primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: A delayed autoimmune response after group A Streptococcus infection causes inflammatory disease involving joints, heart, CNS, and skin; carditis commonly affects the mitral valve.
vignette: A 12-year-old girl develops fever and migratory pain and swelling of the knees and ankles 3 weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis. Examination reveals a new apical holosystolic murmur.
distractor_notes: Septic arthritis usually affects one joint intensely and does not explain migratory polyarthritis plus post-streptococcal carditis.
Viral myocarditis can follow infection but does not characteristically cause migratory large-joint arthritis after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
Serum sickness can cause fever and arthralgia but is typically related to immune-complex reactions to drugs or antigens rather than the classic post-streptococcal Jones pattern.
Infective endocarditis can produce a murmur and systemic illness but does not characteristically cause this delayed migratory large-joint syndrome after strep throat.
key_expl: Delayed illness after group A strep with migratory large-joint arthritis and carditis is classic acute rheumatic fever.
objective: Recognize acute rheumatic fever as a delayed autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal infection.
clues: migratory large-joint arthritis with new murmur

sources.title: Clinical Guidance for Acute Rheumatic Fever
sources.support: CDC describes acute rheumatic fever as a delayed autoimmune sequela of group A strep, usually 1–5 weeks later, with migratory large-joint arthritis and carditis.

sources.title: Diagnosing Acute Rheumatic Fever
sources.support: CDC describes the revised Jones criteria and the need for evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Inflammation of the myocardium, often after viral infection, can directly and immune-mediately injure cardiac muscle and produce chest pain, arrhythmias, ventricular dysfunction, or heart failure.
vignette: A 29-year-old man develops chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and reduced left-ventricular ejection fraction 1 week after a febrile viral illness. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary disease.
distractor_notes: Endocarditis primarily infects the endocardial surface/valves and is associated with bacteremia and valvular findings.
Stable angina produces exertional ischemic symptoms from coronary disease rather than new systolic dysfunction after a viral syndrome.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a structural genetic cardiomyopathy and is not typically preceded by an acute viral illness.
Aortic dissection causes abrupt tearing pain and vascular findings rather than postviral myocardial inflammation.
key_expl: New myocardial dysfunction and chest symptoms after a viral illness without obstructive coronary disease strongly suggest myocarditis.
objective: Recognize myocarditis from postinfectious myocardial inflammation and new ventricular dysfunction.
clues: new reduced ejection fraction without obstructive CAD

sources.title: Myocarditis
sources.support: MedlinePlus defines myocarditis as inflammation of the heart muscle, often caused by viral infection, and describes chest pain, tachycardia, dyspnea, arrhythmia, and heart failure.

sources.title: Heart Inflammation
sources.support: NHLBI describes myocarditis as inflammation of heart muscle that can affect pumping and electrical activity.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: In third-degree AV block, atrial impulses fail to conduct to the ventricles, so atria and ventricles beat independently and a slow escape rhythm maintains ventricular activity.
vignette: A 78-year-old man has recurrent syncope and a pulse of 32/min. ECG shows regular P waves at 78/min and regular QRS complexes at 32/min with no consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes.
distractor_notes: First-degree AV block has prolonged but consistent AV conduction with every P wave followed by a QRS.
Second-degree block intermittently fails to conduct atrial impulses but retains some conducted P-QRS relationships.
Sinus bradycardia preserves a P wave before each QRS with a slow sinus rate.
Atrial fibrillation has disorganized atrial activity without regular P waves.
key_expl: AV dissociation with regular independent atrial and ventricular rhythms is complete heart block.
objective: Identify complete heart block from atrioventricular dissociation and a slow ventricular escape rhythm.
clues: P waves and QRS complexes independent

sources.title: Arrhythmias - Conduction Disorders
sources.support: NHLBI states that third-degree or complete heart block occurs when no atrial electrical signals reach the ventricles and can cause profound bradycardia and syncope.

sources.title: Heart block
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes heart block as slowed or failed conduction to the ventricles and identifies third-degree block as the most severe form.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: In second-degree AV block, some atrial impulses are conducted to the ventricles while others fail, producing intermittent dropped ventricular beats.
vignette: A 66-year-old man taking an AV nodal–blocking medication has intermittent dizziness. ECG shows regular atrial P waves, but every few beats a P wave is not followed by a QRS complex; other P waves conduct to the ventricles.
lead: Which conduction disorder is most likely?
distractor_notes: First-degree AV block conducts every atrial impulse despite prolonged AV delay.
Complete AV block has no consistent conduction of atrial impulses to the ventricles and produces AV dissociation.
Sinus arrest is failure of sinus impulse generation rather than intermittent failure of AV conduction after visible P waves.
Ventricular fibrillation produces chaotic ventricular electrical activity without organized QRS complexes.
key_expl: Intermittent failure of visible atrial impulses to reach the ventricles defines second-degree AV block.
objective: Differentiate second-degree AV block from first-degree and complete heart block by intermittent conduction failure.
clues: some P waves not followed by QRS

sources.title: Heart block
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that in second-degree heart block some electrical impulses may not reach the ventricles, causing missed beats and a slow or irregular rhythm.

sources.title: Arrhythmias - Conduction Disorders
sources.support: NHLBI describes AV block as impaired electrical signal travel from atria through the AV conduction system to the ventricles.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Chaotic ventricular electrical activation causes the ventricles to quiver rather than contract effectively, abruptly eliminating cardiac output and causing cardiac arrest.
vignette: A 63-year-old man collapses and is pulseless. The monitor shows a chaotic irregular waveform with no organized QRS complexes.
lead: Which mechanical consequence is occurring in the ventricles?
correct: Quivering without effective pumping of blood
distractors: Synchronized atrial contraction against closed AV valves
Slow but coordinated ventricular contraction from an escape focus
Normal ventricular contraction with only atrial standstill
distractor_notes: Ventricular fibrillation is not coordinated atrial activity against the ventricles.
A ventricular escape rhythm can be slow but organized and may still generate a pulse.
Normal ventricular contraction is absent in VF because ventricular electrical activity is chaotic.
Fixed outflow obstruction does not explain chaotic electrical activity and sudden pulselessness.
key_expl: In ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles quiver instead of contracting, so effective blood flow ceases.
objective: Explain cardiac arrest in ventricular fibrillation through loss of coordinated ventricular contraction.

sources.title: Cardiac arrest
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that in ventricular fibrillation the lower chambers quiver instead of beating regularly, so the heart cannot pump blood and cardiac arrest results.

sources.title: Arrhythmia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes ventricular fibrillation as a dangerous arrhythmia that can cause sudden cardiac arrest.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, creating parallel rather than serial circulations; survival depends on mixing through an ASD, VSD, or PDA until definitive repair.
vignette: A cyanotic newborn has severe hypoxemia within minutes of birth. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle.
lead: Which additional lesion would most improve systemic oxygenation before definitive repair?
correct: A communication that permits mixing between the two circulations
distractors: Complete closure of the ductus arteriosus
Closure of an atrial septal defect
Elimination of a ventricular septal defect
Further separation of pulmonary and systemic blood
distractor_notes: Ductus closure reduces available mixing and can worsen hypoxemia.
Closing an ASD removes a route for oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix.
Closing a VSD similarly removes a route of mixing.
The fundamental problem is already excessive separation into parallel circuits; further separation worsens oxygen delivery.
key_expl: In d-TGA the systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel, so intercirculatory mixing through ASD/VSD/PDA is temporarily lifesaving.
objective: Explain why shunts that permit mixing improve oxygenation in d-TGA.
clues: aorta from RV and pulmonary artery from LV

sources.title: Dextro-Transposition of the Great Arteries (d-TGA)
sources.support: CDC explains that the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched in d-TGA and that ASD, VSD, or PDA allows blood mixing so oxygen-rich blood can reach the body.

sources.title: Specific Congenital Heart Defects
sources.support: CDC identifies d-TGA as a congenital defect in which the heart's two main arteries are transposed.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Failure of the embryonic outflow vessel to separate completely leaves a single common arterial trunk, usually with a VSD, causing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and excessive pulmonary blood flow.
vignette: A newborn has cyanosis, tachypnea, poor feeding, and a single large arterial vessel arising from the heart. Echocardiography also shows a ventricular septal defect.
lead: Which developmental error best explains this defect?
correct: Failure of the common outflow vessel to separate into the aorta and pulmonary artery
distractors: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth
Failure of the atrial septum to form only
Abnormal fusion of the endocardial cushions only
Premature closure of the foramen ovale
distractor_notes: PDA persistence leaves an abnormal connection between already separated aorta and pulmonary artery rather than one common trunk.
An isolated atrial septal defect does not create a single arterial trunk.
Endocardial cushion defects produce AV septal abnormalities, not a persistent common outflow vessel.
Foramen ovale closure does not determine separation of the aorta and pulmonary artery.
key_expl: Truncus arteriosus results when the developing common outflow vessel fails to separate into aorta and pulmonary artery.
objective: Link a single common arterial trunk plus VSD to failed outflow-tract separation.

sources.title: Truncus Arteriosus
sources.support: CDC states that truncus arteriosus occurs when the developing vessel fails to separate completely, leaving one common vessel and usually a VSD with blood mixing.

sources.title: Specific Congenital Heart Defects
sources.support: CDC identifies truncus arteriosus as a defect in which a single common vessel exits the heart instead of two.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: A reentrant or focal tachyarrhythmia originating above the ventricles produces sudden episodes of rapid regular heart rate that begin and end abruptly.
vignette: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of abrupt-onset palpitations and lightheadedness lasting 10–20 minutes. During an episode her pulse is regular at 190/min; between episodes her ECG and pulse are normal.
distractor_notes: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular rather than a regular narrow-complex paroxysmal tachycardia.
Sinus tachycardia usually changes gradually in response to a physiologic trigger rather than starting and stopping abruptly.
Ventricular fibrillation causes pulseless collapse, not self-limited regular palpitations.
Complete heart block causes bradycardia and AV dissociation.
key_expl: Abrupt recurrent episodes of a rapid regular rhythm originating above the ventricles are characteristic of PSVT.
objective: Recognize PSVT from sudden-onset/sudden-offset rapid regular tachycardia with normal rhythm between episodes.
clues: regular rate ~190 with normal rhythm between episodes

sources.title: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT)
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes PSVT as episodes of rapid heart rate originating above the ventricles that start and stop suddenly, with normal rhythm between episodes.

sources.title: Arrhythmias
sources.support: NHLBI describes supraventricular tachycardias as fast rhythms arising from the atria or AV conduction system.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Congenital narrowing of the pulmonary valve obstructs right-ventricular ejection into the pulmonary artery, increasing right-ventricular pressure and potentially causing right-sided hypertrophy and symptoms with exertion.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy has exertional dyspnea and a systolic ejection murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border. Echocardiography shows a narrowed pulmonary valve with increased right-ventricular systolic pressure.
lead: Which hemodynamic abnormality is most directly produced by this lesion?
correct: Increased resistance to right-ventricular outflow into the pulmonary artery
distractors: Increased resistance to left-ventricular outflow into the aorta
Regurgitant flow from the aorta into the left ventricle
Left-to-right flow through an atrial septal defect
Obstruction of pulmonary venous return to the left atrium
distractor_notes: Left-ventricular outflow obstruction is characteristic of aortic stenosis, not pulmonic stenosis.
Aortic regurgitation is a diastolic left-sided valve lesion.
An ASD can coexist with other defects but is not the primary hemodynamic consequence of pulmonary-valve narrowing.
Pulmonary venous obstruction is anatomically downstream from the lungs and unrelated to pulmonary-valve opening.
key_expl: A narrowed pulmonary valve directly impedes blood flow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery, raising right-ventricular pressure.
objective: Explain the hemodynamic consequence of pulmonic valve stenosis.
clues: narrowed pulmonary valve with elevated RV pressure

sources.title: Pulmonic valve stenosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that pulmonic stenosis narrows the valve between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery, reducing blood flow to the lungs and potentially enlarging the right heart.

sources.title: Specific Congenital Heart Defects
sources.support: CDC provides current congenital heart-defect context and identifies defects that obstruct pulmonary outflow.
